evidence.claim: An early freeway follows the Arroyo Seco through tunnels and tight interchanges
evidence.quote: It connects Los Angeles with Pasadena alongside the Arroyo Seco seasonal river.

evidence.claim: through tunnels
evidence.quote: the northbound lanes pass through the four Figueroa Street Tunnels

evidence.claim: tight interchanges
evidence.quote: folded diamond interchanges that feature extremely tight (right-in/right-out) curves on the exit and entrance ramps.

evidence.claim: The Arroyo Seco Parkway connects Los Angeles and Pasadena beside a seasonal river, with northbound tunnels through Elysian Park and tight entrance and exit curves.
evidence.quote: It connects Los Angeles with Pasadena alongside the Arroyo Seco seasonal river.

evidence.claim: An archived Federal Highway Administration profile describes this National Scenic Byway as a blend of landscaped parkway and modern freeway, passing through the Arroyo Seco’s historic Arts and Crafts landscape.
evidence.quote: The Arroyo Seco Parkway connects Los Angeles and Pasadena through the historic Arts and Crafts landscape of the Arroyo Seco.

evidence.claim: National Scenic Byway
evidence.quote: National Scenic Byway • California

evidence.claim: blend of landscaped parkway and modern freeway
evidence.quote: Conceived in the parkway tradition with gentle curves, lush landscaping, and scenic vistas, the byway incorporated the modern elements that would lay the groundwork for the California freeway system.

evidence.claim: Early plans competed over the road’s purpose: recreation in a park setting or a fast connection between the cities.
evidence.quote: some, influenced by the City Beautiful movement, concentrated on the park, while others, particularly those backed by the Automobile Club of Southern California (ACSC), had as their primary purpose a fast road connecting the two cities.

evidence.claim: By the mid-1930s, commuter needs had overtaken the recreational emphasis.
evidence.quote: By the mid-1930s, plans for a primarily recreational parkway had been overshadowed by the need to carry large numbers of commuters.

evidence.claim: Construction began in 1938, and most of the parkway opened in 1940.
evidence.quote: began with a groundbreaking ceremony in South Pasadena on March 22, 1938

evidence.claim: most of the parkway opened in 1940
evidence.quote: Mostly opened in 1940

evidence.claim: Engineers designed for 45 miles per hour, retaining parkway features such as roadside native plantings.
evidence.quote: The engineers used a design speed of 45 miles per hour

evidence.claim: roadside native plantings
evidence.quote: plantings of mostly native flora alongside the road.

evidence.claim: Local streets sometimes served as ramps, ending in sharp right turns where a conventional interchange would not fit.
evidence.quote: where local streets often took the place of dedicated ramps, ending at the parkway with a sharp right turn required to enter or exit.

evidence.claim: where a conventional interchange would not fit
evidence.quote: Although, in some areas, it was possible to use a standard diamond interchange, other locations required folded diamonds

evidence.claim: Northbound, begin at the Four Level Interchange, pass through the Figueroa Street Tunnels and cross the Los Angeles River.
evidence.quote: The six-lane Arroyo Seco Parkway (part of State Route 110) begins at the Four Level Interchange

evidence.claim: cross the Los Angeles River
evidence.quote: the Arroyo Seco Parkway crosses a pair of three-lane bridges over the Los Angeles River

evidence.claim: The original road then follows the Arroyo Seco’s west bank, passing beneath the Santa Fe railroad bridge before crossing the stream into South Pasadena.
evidence.quote: Here the original 1940 freeway, mostly built along the west bank of the Arroyo Seco, begins

evidence.claim: passing beneath the Santa Fe railroad bridge
evidence.quote: crosses the Arroyo Seco Parkway at an elevation of over 56 feet

evidence.claim: crossing the stream into South Pasadena
evidence.quote: the Arroyo Seco Parkway instead curves east, crossing the stream into South Pasadena.

evidence.claim: Beyond Fair Oaks Avenue it turns north past Raymond Hill and reaches Pasadena.
evidence.quote: Beyond Fair Oaks Avenue, SR 110 curves north around the east side of Raymond Hill and enters Pasadena

evidence.claim: The freeway ends at Glenarm Street; Arroyo Parkway continues as a city street toward Colorado Boulevard.
evidence.quote: The freeway, and state maintenance, ends at the intersection with Glenarm Street

evidence.claim: Arroyo Parkway continues as a city street toward Colorado Boulevard
evidence.quote: continues north as a surface road to Colorado Boulevard (historic U.S. Route 66)

evidence.claim: Four tunnels carry northbound State Route 110 through Elysian Park.
evidence.quote: The Figueroa Street Tunnels are a set of four four-lane tunnels that carry northbound traffic on State Route 110 (the Arroyo Seco Parkway) through Elysian Park

evidence.claim: They began as a two-way road, with two lanes in each direction and a sidewalk along one side.
evidence.quote: From opening, the tunnels carried two lanes in each direction, with a 5-foot (1.5 m) sidewalk on the side.

evidence.claim: The three northern tunnels opened in 1931 to provide a bypass of part of North Broadway.
evidence.quote: The north three tunnels opened in 1931 as a bypass to a section of North Broadway

evidence.claim: Once the parkway reached them, its six lanes narrowed to four at the tunnels and viaduct.
evidence.quote: the six-lane parkway narrowed to four lanes at the viaduct and through the tunnels

evidence.claim: A separate southbound road opened in 1943, leaving the older tunnels for northbound travel.
evidence.quote: The two-way Figueroa Street Tunnels and Viaduct were repurposed for four lanes of northbound traffic, and a higher southbound roadway was built to the west.

evidence.claim: A separate southbound road opened in 1943
evidence.quote: This new road opened December 30, 1943.

evidence.claim: The newer southbound lanes run higher through open cuts and cross the valleys between ridges on viaducts.
evidence.quote: Through Elysian Park, it was built higher than the tunnels, with open-cuts through the ridges through which the older tunnels were built, and viaducts over the valleys between the ridges.

evidence.claim: Above the parkway in Highland Park, the Santa Fe Arroyo Seco Railroad Bridge carries Metro’s A Line.
evidence.quote: The A Line now runs on the bridge's tracks following the Regional Connector's opening in June 2023.

evidence.claim: Highland Park
evidence.quote: The Santa Fe Arroyo Seco Railroad Bridge in Highland Park, Los Angeles

evidence.claim: The span extends more than 710 feet and crosses the road at an elevation of over 56 feet.
evidence.quote: is more than 710 feet (220 m) long and crosses the Arroyo Seco Parkway at an elevation of over 56 feet (17 m).

evidence.claim: It replaced an 1889 wooden trestle, itself a replacement for an 1885 crossing.
evidence.quote: replaced the 1889 wooden trestle used by the Southern California Railway

evidence.claim: itself a replacement for an 1885 crossing
evidence.quote: replaced the original 1885 wooden trestle bridge built by the Los Angeles and San Gabriel Valley Railroad.

evidence.claim: Mainline rail service ended in 1994.
evidence.quote: Mainline rail service ended in 1994.

evidence.claim: The bridge was then retrofitted for the Gold Line, which opened in 2003; the A Line took over these tracks after the Regional Connector opened in June 2023.
evidence.quote: In the late 1990s, the bridge was retrofitted to accommodate Gold Line of the Los Angeles Metro Rail system, which opened on July 26, 2003.

evidence.claim: The older wooden crossings carried the Southern California Railway and, before it, the Los Angeles and San Gabriel Valley Railroad.
evidence.quote: the 1889 wooden trestle used by the Southern California Railway

evidence.claim: the Los Angeles and San Gabriel Valley Railroad
evidence.quote: the original 1885 wooden trestle bridge built by the Los Angeles and San Gabriel Valley Railroad.

evidence.claim: At Glenarm Street, freeway driving gives way to Arroyo Parkway, a surface street continuing toward Colorado Boulevard.
evidence.quote: The freeway, and state maintenance, ends at the intersection with Glenarm Street, but the six- and four-lane Arroyo Parkway, now maintained by the city of Pasadena, continues north as a surface road to Colorado Boulevard

evidence.claim: Colorado Boulevard and Arroyo Parkway once carried U.S. Route 66 through Pasadena.
evidence.quote: The historic highway entered Pasadena from the east on Colorado Boulevard and then jogged south on Arroyo Parkway

evidence.claim: An earlier transport connection had helped reshape the city: Santa Fe service began stopping downtown in 1887, triggering a real-estate boom.
evidence.quote: In 1887, the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway opened the Second District of the Los Angeles Division and began making stops at the Santa Fe Depot in downtown Pasadena. This triggered a real estate boom.

evidence.claim: Pasadena developed as a winter resort for wealthy Easterners, with new neighborhoods, business districts and links to Los Angeles.
evidence.quote: Pasadena became a winter resort for wealthy Easterners, spurring the development of new neighborhoods and business districts, and increased road and transit connections with Los Angeles.

evidence.claim: Rail travel preceded the parkway link, which connected the city to downtown Los Angeles in 1940.
evidence.quote: In 1940, when the Arroyo Seco Parkway, California's first freeway, connected Pasadena to Downtown Los Angeles.

evidence.claim: Old Pasadena is the city’s original commercial district.
evidence.quote: Old Pasadena is the city's original commercial district.

flags: Tunnel page conflicts internally on the fourth tunnel (1935 versus 1936) and viaduct (1943 versus 1937); these dates omitted. Parkway and bridge pages disagree on railroad bridge construction (1895 versus 1896); date omitted.
Tunnel decorations are described in the past tense, without a clear statement that all eight seals survive; no present-day notice asserts their survival.
The current nine-mile tagline is overgeneralized: archived FHWA lists 9.5 miles and material maps 9.4; route length omitted. The road was mostly opened in 1940, with later extensions.

The only cached official byway profile is archived. Its non-peak travel-time estimate and Wikipedia’s truck restriction lack current operator confirmation; neither is supplied as current practical advice.
Driving order follows the cached parkway route description between the material’s southern starting area and Pasadena at mile 9.39.
